title: Carousel of Progress video:  @Joe Weinberg #theatre #experimental #pl...
transcript: Can you have live theater without live actors? And if so, does that make me a hypocrite? A couple months ago, I posted a kind of snarky, disdainful video, which I'll link in the caption, about the Carousel of Progress at Disney World. Nothing against the attraction itself, but the fact that they claim to be “the longest running stage show in the history of American theater.” I said, that's ridiculous. It's like calling Chuck E. Cheese “the longest running concert in music history” But even in that video, I admitted there are times when I consider something theatre, even when there are no live actors, but only if there's an interactive component where you can kind of say that the audience is stepping into the role of the performer. But now I'm even questioning that, because this week I attended All That Fall at the Under the Radar festival, and it's a rendition of a Samuel Beckett radio play, where it is still pre-recorded by actors who are not in the building. But it's played over this large diorama of the town where it takes place, and they use, sometimes, lighting to sort of direct your attention around the diorama. Based on my earlier definition, there's no reason to count this as theater and not Carousel of Progress. And yet I am counting this as theatre. I put it on my list of shows that I saw this week. I wrote about it in my theatre journal. And as much as I do enjoy nitpicking and semantics, you know, that's why I'm “Overthinking Theatre.” I am also a believer that language is kind of fluid. Words are defined by how we use them. So after some reflection, I maybe gonna revise my little rule and say that the reason that I would call this theatre and not carousel of progress is context. This is being put on by Mabou Mines, a theater company at the Under the Radar Theatre Festival. It's being done in a theatre I received a program. It was created by Joanne Akalaitis, a theatre artist. And even though it wasn't written for the stage, it was written by Samuel Beckett, who is first and foremost a very famous playwright. Whereas Carousel of Progress is in a theme park. It was created by Imagineers. The unconventional venue that moves the audience around in a circle is very innovative, but it makes it feel more like a ride than like a play. Recently, I was learning about the prototype theory in linguistics, where we make associations less by hard boundaries between categories and more about what feels, vibe-wise, closer to the quintessential example of that thing. And here it's like going to All That Fall felt more like going to a play than Carousel of Progress. But I still stand by everything I said in my other video. I think this record is very stupid.
classificationReason: Philosophical discussion about what constitutes live theater, using 'All That Fall' at Under the Radar festival as a case study. That show is not on the list, and the primary content is conceptual, not a production review.
